title: The Dirty Secret of Forward Deployed Engineering — Natalie Meurer, Sierra

primary.label: Coding Agents & Software Engineering
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 49%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk discusses engineering roles and practices across multiple application domains—law enforcement, defense, aerospace (Airbus), and customer experience—without focusing on any single application vertical. The core subject is the discipline and evolution of forward deployed engineering as a cross-domain practice.

domains.label: Developer Platforms
domains.rationale: The talk references Foundry and Slate as developer platforms that FDEs built on and enabled customers to use, and discusses the tooling ecosystem that supports deployed engineering work across its historical evolution.

domains.label: Enterprise Operations
domains.rationale: The talk discusses enterprise customer deployments, platform stability operations (DevOps), and customer enablement within large organizations like Airbus. The operational aspects of FDE—firefighting infrastructure, managing on-prem deployments, and enabling enterprise customers—are significant themes.

summary: Natalie Meurer, Head of Agent Engineering at Sierra, delivered this talk at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 (June 29–July 2, Moscone West, San Francisco). She traces the evolution of Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE) from its Palantir origins, arguing the 'dirty secret' is that FDE never settled into a single discipline—it accumulated DevOps, data integration, ontology work in Slate and Foundry, solution architecture, and customer enablement until the label lost clear meaning. She identifies four FDE vintages: (1) 2008–2012: platform stability and on-prem DevOps, where engineers physically deployed to customer sites; (2) 2012–2016: data integration and ontology modeling, filling the gap between stable platforms and empty data pipelines; (3) 2016–2020: custom solutions via Slate (a drag-and-drop builder similar to Retool) and the Foundry era emphasizing data-to-decision-making with write-back dashboards; (4) 2020+: customer enablement, exemplified by Airbus Skywise enabling thousands of engineers on Foundry. These jobs accumulated rather than replacing each other, creating distinct FDE vintages and making FDE the best generalist training ground. Meurer identifies customer accountability as the one continuity across all vintages. She argues that as coding agents make writing code cheap, FDEs can now build end-to-end solutions rather than just prototype, and product engineering is becoming more client-facing, blurring the lines between roles. She connects pricing models to accountability: seat-based assumes a tool, usage-based is hard to attribute to outcomes, and outcome-based (as Sierra uses) puts you on the hook for results. She revises her July 2024 framing of agent engineering as a subdiscipline of AI engineering, now arguing it is a flavor of FDE focused on outcomes. Her broader thesis: everything is trending toward FDE—product, agent, AI, solutions, and customer engineering all involve building and deploying on behalf of customers. She concludes: 'Forward deployed engineering is dead. And long live forward deployed engineering.'
whyItMatters: The talk weaves together software engineering evolution and AI engineering emergence through a single thread: customer accountability. The FDE vintage framework (DevOps → data integration → ontology → Slate/Foundry → customer enablement) shows how engineering roles accumulate complexity over time rather than replacing prior work. Coding agents serve as the technological catalyst that transforms this accumulated FDE expertise from prototyping to end-to-end solution delivery, which in turn blurs the boundary between product engineering and deployed engineering. The pricing model analysis (seat vs usage vs outcome) provides the economic lens that connects FDE accountability to modern agent engineering—outcome-based pricing is the financial expression of the same customer accountability that has defined FDE since 2008. Agent engineering is then positioned not as a new discipline but as the latest FDE vintage, one where AI agents are the deployment substrate and outcome accountability is baked into the business model. This unified framing explains why everything is trending toward FDE: the convergence of cheap code (coding agents), customer-facing product engineering, and outcome-based pricing creates conditions where the FDE practice of building and deploying on behalf of customers becomes the dominant engineering paradigm.
temporalContext: This talk was delivered at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026 (June 29–July 2, 2026) and published on YouTube on July 28, 2026. Sierra was founded in 2023, publicly launched in February 2024, and raised nearly $1B by May 2026 reaching a $10B valuation. Meurer started at Sierra in January 2024 and wrote her initial agent engineering article in July 2024, which this talk revises from 'subdiscipline of AI engineering' to 'flavor of FDE.' Palantir, where Meurer worked from 2016–2021, went public in September 2020. The talk reflects a moment when coding agents are rapidly maturing (2025–2026), enterprise AI agent deployment is scaling, and outcome-based pricing models are gaining traction in the AI industry.
takeaways: FDE's dirty secret is that the term accumulated so many meanings it either doesn't exist or exists too much—yet it remains the hottest job in AI
FDE started as DevOps for on-prem platform stability (2008), then grew cumulatively to include data integration (2012), custom solutions via Slate (2016), and customer enablement on Foundry (2020)
The one continuity across all FDE vintages is customer accountability—whether for DevOps, enablement, custom solutioning, or data integration
When code becomes cheap via coding agents, FDEs can build end-to-end solutions rather than just prototype, making them more impactful in product development
Product engineering is becoming more client-facing, blurring the line between it and FDE—good engineers in either role must think about product and customer together
Pricing models reveal accountability structures: seat-based assumes a tool, usage-based is hard to attribute to outcomes, outcome-based puts you on the hook for results
Agent engineering is a flavor of FDE focused on outcomes, not a separate discipline—Sierra's outcome-based pricing reflects this

FDE is dead as a coherent label, but long live FDE as the practice of being accountable to customer outcomes

concepts.name: Agent Engineering
concepts.explanation: Meurer revises her July 2024 framing of agent engineering as a subdiscipline of AI engineering, now arguing it is a flavor of forward deployed engineering focused on outcomes. Sierra uses the 'agent engineer' title intentionally to reflect this accountability orientation.
concepts.importance: Central AI concept of the talk; redefines agent engineering not as a standalone discipline but as an instance of the broader FDE practice with outcome accountability.

concepts.name: Coding Agents
concepts.explanation: AI-powered tools that make writing code cheap, enabling FDEs to build end-to-end solutions rather than just prototype. Meurer argues this transforms FDE impact from prototyping to full solution delivery.
concepts.importance: The technological catalyst that enables the convergence thesis—cheap code means deployed engineers can own the full solution lifecycle, not just the prototype phase.

concepts.name: Harness Engineering
concepts.explanation: A related term to agent engineering that Meurer mentions as contributing to terminology proliferation and confusion in the field. The talk aims to clarify how it relates to FDE and agent engineering.
concepts.importance: Represents the broader landscape of emerging AI engineering role labels that the talk seeks to unify under the FDE framework.

concepts.name: Conversational AI Agents
concepts.explanation: Sierra's product category—AI agents that handle customer experience across voice, chat, email, and WhatsApp channels. The outcome-based pricing model for these agents exemplifies the FDE accountability principle applied to AI products.
concepts.importance: Provides the concrete product context for how agent engineering works in practice at Sierra, grounding the abstract FDE-to-agent-engineering connection in a real deployment.

concepts.name: Agent OS and Agent Studio Platform
concepts.explanation: Sierra's platform products (Agent OS 2.0, Agent Studio 2.0, Agent Data Platform) that the agent engineering team builds on and deploys. The platform enables multi-channel agents with memory, context, and system integrations across 59 languages.
concepts.importance: Represents the tooling substrate that modern agent engineering teams operate on, analogous to how Palantir's Slate and Foundry served earlier FDE vintages.

concepts.name: Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE)
concepts.explanation: A role originating at Palantir where engineers are embedded directly with customers to deploy, integrate, and build solutions. The talk argues FDE accumulated so many responsibilities across historical vintages that the label lost coherent meaning, yet it remains the hottest job in AI.
concepts.importance: Central subject of the talk; the framework through which all other engineering concepts are analyzed and connected.

concepts.name: DevOps and Platform Stability
concepts.explanation: The earliest FDE vintage (2008–2012) was essentially DevOps—physically deploying to customer sites for on-prem installations, with platform stability as the core job. Meurer's onboarding project was deploying software on an EC2 instance, and much of the work involved firefighting customer infrastructure issues.
concepts.importance: Establishes the historical baseline of FDE from which all subsequent vintages evolved, showing how the role began as infrastructure operations.

concepts.name: Data Integration
concepts.explanation: By 2012, Palantir's platform stabilized but lacked integrated data. FDEs took on data integration work, deeply understanding customer environments to model data into ontologies. Meurer compares data integration software without data to a movie theater playing nothing.
concepts.importance: Represents the second FDE vintage and the critical shift from infrastructure-focused work to data-focused work, expanding the FDE skill set.

concepts.name: Ontology (Data Taxonomy)
concepts.explanation: Palantir's term for a structured data taxonomy that FDEs built by modeling customer data into coherent schemas, giving FDEs a dual DevOps-plus-data-integration role.
concepts.importance: Key technical artifact of the data integration era that enabled later solution-building on top of structured data.

concepts.name: FDE Vintages (Cumulative Job Accumulation)
concepts.explanation: The concept that FDE roles accumulated rather than replaced each other across four eras (2008, 2012, 2016, 2020), creating distinct 'vintages' of FDE experience. Meurer uses this as an interview question: 'What vintage of FDE are you?'
concepts.importance: Provides the analytical framework for understanding why FDE job postings today unrealistically combine all historical roles, and why the label has lost coherent meaning.

concepts.name: Foundry and Write-Back Dashboards
concepts.explanation: The Foundry era emphasized going from data to decision-making, with the key insight that dashboards not writing back to data sources decay in usefulness over time. This principle guided how FDEs built decision-support tools.
concepts.importance: Represents a maturation of FDE work from data integration to actionable decision-making, and introduces the write-back principle as a design constraint.

concepts.name: Customer Enablement
concepts.explanation: By 2020, FDE work shifted toward empowering customers to do FDE work themselves, exemplified by Airbus Skywise enabling thousands of Airbus engineers on the Foundry platform. This represents the fourth FDE vintage.
concepts.importance: Represents the latest FDE vintage and the shift from doing-for to enabling customers, which connects to how agent engineering teams scale deployment.

concepts.name: Customer Accountability
concepts.explanation: The one continuity across all FDE vintages—whether DevOps, enablement, custom solutioning, or data integration, FDEs are always accountable to customer outcomes. Meurer identifies this as the defining characteristic that connects FDE to agent engineering.
concepts.importance: The through line that unifies all FDE vintages and provides the bridge to modern agent engineering and outcome-based pricing.

concepts.name: Product Engineering and FDE Convergence
concepts.explanation: Meurer argues product engineering is becoming more client-facing, blurring the line between it and FDE. Good engineers in either role must think about product and customer together, and coding agents accelerate this convergence.
concepts.importance: Challenges the traditional separation between product engineering and deployed engineering, arguing for a unified customer-accountable engineering practice.

concepts.name: Outcome-Based Pricing
concepts.explanation: A pricing model where cost is tied to delivered value—did you make a sale, did you solve a customer's inquiry—rather than seats or usage. Sierra uses this model for customer experience AI, and Meurer predicts most pricing in the market will move toward it.
concepts.importance: Connects pricing structure to accountability, showing that outcome-based pricing aligns with FDE principles of being on the hook for customer results.

concepts.name: Seat-Based and Usage-Based Pricing
concepts.explanation: Seat-based pricing assumes a tool where outcomes are hard to attribute, while usage-based pricing (like what we pay OpenAI or Anthropic) is also hard to attribute to outcomes. These models contrast with outcome-based pricing in their accountability structures.
concepts.importance: Provides the contrast against which outcome-based pricing is argued as superior for FDE-aligned work, completing the pricing-accountability framework.

sections.title: Introduction: speaker background and the dirty secret of FDE
sections.summary: Natalie Meurer introduces herself as head of agent engineering at Sierra, with prior experience at Palantir (2016–2021) in privacy, infrastructure, and FDE roles. She states the dirty secret: FDE doesn't exist as a coherent single discipline because the term describes so many things it means nothing, yet it remains the hottest job in AI.

sections.title: Agent engineering as a subdiscipline of AI engineering
sections.summary: Meurer recounts writing a July 2024 article positioning agent engineering as a subdiscipline of AI engineering with the same customer accountability as FDE but as its own domain. She notes the proliferation of related terms—agent engineering, harness engineering—contributing to confusion the talk aims to clarify.

sections.title: Palantir origins: leading with location and platform stability (2008–2012)
sections.summary: Palantir's 2008–2016 job postings led with location because FDE meant physically sitting with customers at on-prem deployments. The early job was essentially DevOps—platform stability was the bulk of the work. Meurer's onboarding project was deploying software on an EC2 instance, and much of the job involved firefighting customer infrastructure issues.

sections.title: Data integration and the ontology era (2012–2016)
sections.summary: By 2012 the platform stabilized but lacked integrated data—Meurer compares data integration software without data to a movie theater playing nothing. FDEs took on data integration work, deeply understanding customer environments to model data into ontologies (Palantir's term for a data taxonomy), giving FDEs a dual DevOps-plus-data-integration role.

sections.title: Slate, Foundry, and customer enablement (2016–2020)
sections.summary: In 2016, custom solutions emerged via Slate, a drag-and-drop builder similar to Retool, mapping UI components to data sources. Foundry era emphasized data-to-decision-making, with the key insight that dashboards not writing back to data sources decay in usefulness. By 2020, customer enablement became central—empowering customers like Airbus (Skywise) to do FDE work themselves.

sections.title: FDE is not one thing: vintages and today's landscape
sections.summary: Meurer emphasizes these weren't discrete eras—jobs accumulated over time, making FDE the best generalist training ground and explaining Palantir alumni founding success. She introduces the FDE vintage interview question and shows that today's job postings unrealistically combine all historical roles. FDE is everywhere now—Google GCP, OpenAI, and industry leaders all hiring for it, but each describes a different vintage.

sections.title: Customer accountability as the through line when code gets cheap
sections.summary: Meurer identifies customer accountability as the one continuity across all FDE vintages—whether DevOps, enablement, custom solutioning, or data integration. When code becomes cheap via coding agents, FDEs can build end-to-end solutions rather than just prototype, making them more impactful in product development. She observes product engineering is also becoming more client-facing, blurring the lines between roles—good engineers in either role must think about product and customer together.

sections.title: Pricing models: seats vs usage vs outcome
sections.summary: Meurer connects pricing models to accountability structures. Seat-based pricing, the historical default, assumes a tool where outcomes are hard to attribute. Usage-based pricing, like what we pay OpenAI or Anthropic, is also hard to attribute to outcomes. Outcome-based pricing, as Sierra uses for customer experience AI, charges for value delivered—did you make a sale, did you solve a customer's inquiry. She predicts most pricing in this market will move to outcome-based.

sections.title: Agent engineering is FDE reborn
sections.summary: Meurer revises her July 2024 framing: agent engineering is not a separate subdiscipline but a flavor of FDE focused on outcomes. Her broader claim is that everything is trending toward FDE—product engineering, agent engineering, AI engineering, solutions engineering, and customer engineering all involve building and deploying on behalf of customers. She concludes with the paradox: forward deployed engineering is dead as a label, but long live forward deployed engineering as the practice of enabling customer outcomes. She notes Sierra is hiring across FDE roles.

demonstrations: Palantir FDE timeline from 2008 to 2024 showing cumulative job responsibilities across eras
Slate described as a drag-and-drop builder similar to Retool for mapping UI components to data sources
Foundry's principle that dashboards must write back to data sources to remain useful over time
Airbus Skywise example: enabling thousands of Airbus engineers on Foundry to do FDE work themselves
Pricing model spectrum from seat-based to usage-based to outcome-based, with agents pushing toward outcome-based
limitations: The FDE label has become so broad across companies that it no longer has a single clear meaning
Today's combined FDE job postings require unrealistic combinations of experience (staff eng, direct sales, solution architecture, teaching)
Outcome-based pricing is not always possible—only works when you can attribute outcomes to the product
quantitativeClaims: Natalie worked at Palantir from 2016 to 2021
Natalie has been at Sierra from 2024 to 2026
She wrote an article on agent engineering in July 2024, about 6 months after starting at Sierra
Palantir was on the verge of IPO around 2020

organization.name: Sierra
organization.summary: Sierra is a conversational AI platform company co-founded by Bret Taylor (former Salesforce Co-CEO, OpenAI board chair) and Clay Bavor (former Google Labs head) in 2023, headquartered in San Francisco, California. The company builds and deploys AI agents for enterprise customer experience through its Agent OS platform, serving industries including financial services, healthcare, telecommunications, travel and hospitality, and retail. Sierra works with 40% of Fortune 50 companies including ADT, Chime, Cigna, Nordstrom, Nubank, and Wayfair. The company has raised approximately $1.585B in total funding, reaching a $10B valuation as of 2026. Natalie Meurer, Head of Agent Engineering at Sierra, leads a global team of more than 120 engineers building conversational AI agents and delivered this talk at the AI Engineer World's Fair 2026. Sierra uses outcome-based pricing where customers pay for resolved outcomes rather than tokens, exemplifying the FDE accountability principle discussed in the talk.

technologies.label: Forward Deployed Engineering (FDE)
technologies.summary: Forward Deployed Engineering is an engineering practice originating at Palantir where engineers are embedded directly with customers to deploy, integrate, and build solutions. The talk argues FDE accumulated so many responsibilities across four historical vintages (2008 DevOps, 2012 data integration, 2016 Slate/Foundry custom solutions, 2020 customer enablement) that the label lost coherent meaning. The one continuity is customer accountability, being on the hook for outcomes, which connects FDE to modern agent engineering. Meurer revises her July 2024 framing of agent engineering as a subdiscipline of AI engineering, now arguing it is a flavor of FDE focused on outcomes. Her broader thesis: everything is trending toward FDE.
technologies.role: Primary subject; defines the entire narrative arc from Palantir origins to modern agent engineering convergence, including the conclusion that FDE is dead as a label but alive as a practice

technologies.label: Palantir Foundry and Slate Platform
technologies.summary: Palantir Foundry is the data integration and decision-making platform that FDEs built on and enabled customers to use across multiple FDE vintages. The Foundry era emphasized going from data to decision-making, with the key insight that dashboards not writing back to data sources decay in usefulness. Slate, a drag-and-drop builder similar to Retool, enabled FDEs to map UI components to data sources for custom solutions. Together, Foundry and Slate represent the platform substrate for FDE work from 2012 through 2020, including the Airbus Skywise customer enablement example where thousands of Airbus engineers were enabled on Foundry.
technologies.role: Historical platform context; illustrates the tooling evolution across FDE vintages from data integration through customer enablement, and provides the analogy for how Sierra's Agent OS serves modern agent engineers

technologies.label: Sierra Agent Platform (Agent OS)
technologies.summary: Sierra's Agent OS is the conversational AI platform that the speaker's agent engineering team of 120+ engineers builds on and deploys. The platform includes Agent Studio 2.0 for agent configuration, Agent Data Platform for memory and context, and supports multi-channel agents across 59 languages with both volume-based and outcome-based pricing. This platform represents the modern tooling substrate for agent engineering, analogous to how Palantir's Foundry and Slate served earlier FDE vintages. The outcome-based pricing model exemplifies the FDE principle of customer accountability applied to AI products.
technologies.role: Modern platform context; exemplifies the convergence of agent engineering with FDE through outcome-based pricing and customer accountability, serving as the present-day contrast to Palantir's historical FDE platforms

technologies.label: Coding Agents
technologies.summary: Coding agents are AI-powered tools that make writing code cheap, enabling forward deployed engineers to build end-to-end solutions rather than just prototype. Meurer identifies this as the technological catalyst that transforms FDE impact from prototyping to full solution delivery, and as a force blurring the boundary between product engineering and deployed engineering. When code becomes cheap, good engineers in either role must think about product and customer together, making the FDE practice of building and deploying on behalf of customers the dominant engineering paradigm.
technologies.role: Catalyst technology; the factor that transforms FDE from prototyping to end-to-end solution delivery and drives convergence between product engineering and deployed engineering
